The 13 baseline-only trials (1.6%) were spread across 8 sessions, and no participant gave baseline-only responses throughout a session (maximum 3 of 12 excerpts; individual means ≥ 1.21; peak ratings of 3-5), which suggests that low ratings reflected stimulus-specific neutrality rather than inattention. Although responses concentrate at baseline (45.5% of all 7,344 individual category ratings; up to 65.9% for Tenderness), we assessed potential distortions from unequal category spacing and floor effects with crossed ordinal Cumulative Link Mixed Models (CLMMs; Section 2.5).

2.4. Statistical Modeling: Crossed Linear Mixed-Effects Models (LMMs) and Variance Partitioning

Each listening session covered the 12 tracks of one survey version, so the 816 ratings (68 sessions from 65 participants, 36 tracks) are grouped in two crossed ways: by participant and by track. Ratings from the same participant share that person's scale use and baseline bias, and ratings of the same track share acoustic attributes that the predictor does not capture. Standard linear regression and common machine-learning models treat observations as independent; ignoring this double clustering inflates Type I error and confounds stimulus-driven effects with listener response bias (Judd et al., 2012). We therefore fitted crossed LMMs (Baayen et al., 2008), which model participant and track variability explicitly.

Rather than fitting a single saturated multivariate model, which would over-parameterize the stimulus space relative to the number of tracks (N = 36), inflate variance (multicollinearity), and obscure individual psychoacoustic relationships, we evaluated each of the 19 curated descriptors in a separate marginal LMM for each of the 9 GEMS dimensions (19 ×9 = 171 models). Acoustic predictors were re-standardized (z-scores, M = 0, SD = 1) across the 36 evaluated tracks before model fitting, whereas ratings remained on their original 1-5 scale. The fixed-effect slope β₁ therefore represents the expected change in Likert rating per +1 SD in the descriptor, which allows effect sizes to be compared across physical units.

On unaggregated trial-level data (N = 816), each model was specified as: where: • 𝑌 𝑖𝑗𝑘 is the Likert rating (1-5) assigned by participant 𝑖to musical excerpt 𝑗in survey version 𝑘.

• 𝛽 0 is the global fixed intercept.

• 𝑋 𝑗 is the standardized acoustic descriptor for excerpt 𝑗, with 𝛽 1 denoting the fixedeffect slope of interest.

• 𝑉 𝑖𝑗𝑘 is the dummy-coded categorical covariate controlling for survey version (Version 1 serving as reference).

• 𝑢 𝑖 part ∼ 𝒩(0, 𝜎 partfoot_0 ) is the random intercept for participant 𝑖, capturing individual baseline calibration and response bias.

• 𝑤 𝑗 track ∼ 𝒩(0, 𝜎 track 2 ) is the crossed random intercept for musical track 𝑗, accounting for stimulus-specific variance beyond 𝑋 𝑗.

• 𝜀 𝑖𝑗𝑘 ∼ 𝒩(0, 𝜎 𝜀 2 ) is the residual error (combining participant x track interaction and measurement noise).

Models were fitted by restricted maximum likelihood (REML). Because acoustic features vary across tracks (N = 36) and not across individual trials, tests of β₁ used Student's t distribution with conservative track-level degrees of freedom (𝑑𝑓 = 𝑁 tracks -𝑝 fixed = 36 -4 = 32; intercept, β₁, and two survey-version parameters), which avoids the anticonservative bias of asymptotic normal approximations. Multiple testing across the 171 models was controlled with the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) procedure at 0.05. Sensitivity analyses of alternative degrees of freedom and randomslope structures are described in Section 2.5.

To quantify the relative contributions of acoustic stimuli and listener bias, we partitioned variance using null models, which keep survey version and the crossed random intercepts but omit the acoustic predictor. For each GEMS dimension, total rating variance was decomposed into stimulus consensus (track intraclass correlation coefficient, ICC track = survey version was entered as a fixed effect, these shares are conditional on survey version (the variance it explains is not included in the denominator). Approximate twosided 95% confidence intervals were obtained with a two-way cluster bootstrap that resampled tracks and participants with replacement within survey versions (B = 1,000 iterations per dimension; 9,000 fits in total). Because dual-factor resampling alters cell structures, the replicate distributions were bias-corrected (shifted so that replicate means matched the point estimates) and clipped to [0, 1].

2.5. Sensitivity and robustness analyses

To verify that the primary trial-level LMM inferences were robust to data aggregation, response-scale discretization, degrees-of-freedom approximations, and random-effects structure, we ran three complementary analyses.

Track-level consensus. Consensus ratings were computed as the arithmetic mean of participant scores for each of the 36 evaluated tracks. Pearson correlations (r) were computed between each of the 19 standardized descriptors and each of the nine GEMS dimensions (171 pairs), with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR control (0.05). This analysis tests whether stimulus-level profiles converge with the trial-level LMMs when listener variance is averaged out, and it allows direct comparison with MIR studies that rely on aggregated stimulus norms (e.g., Strauss et al., 2024; Zentner et al., 2008). Because survey versions are confounded with the evaluated track subsets and cannot be entered as a covariate at the stimulus level, we additionally computed partial correlations after residualizing both acoustic and emotional variables on survey version (df = 32).

Ordinal modeling. Because GEMS-9 ratings are discrete 5-point Likert responses, we tested whether treating them as continuous in linear LMMs introduced distortion from unequal category spacing or floor effects (baseline responses were 45% of ratings, 66% for Tenderness). All 171 pairs were re-estimated with CLMMs (logit link) and the same crossed random-effects structure: logit[𝑃(𝑌 𝑖𝑗𝑘 ≤ 𝑐)] = 𝜃 𝑐 -(𝛽 1 𝑋 𝑗 + ∑ 𝛽 2,𝑘 3 𝑘=2 𝑉 𝑖𝑗𝑘 + 𝑢 𝑖 part + 𝑤 𝑗 track ) where θc are the threshold cut-points between response categories c ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4}, and the remaining terms mirror the primary crossed LMM specification (see Section 2.4).

Slopes were exponentiated to odds ratios (OR = exp(β₁)), the multiplicative change in the odds of a higher rating per +1 SD in the descriptor. Because Python statistical libraries do not support crossed-random-effects ordinal models, CLMMs were fitted in R with the clmm function of the ordinal package (maximum likelihood, Laplace approximation).

Inference used stimulus-level Student's t tests (df = 32), consistent with the primary LMMs, alongside asymptotic Wald z tests and likelihood-ratio tests for singular fits, with FDR control (0.05) across all 171 ordinal models.

Alternative LMM specifications.

To confirm that the primary results do not depend on the conservative df = 32 heuristic or on omitting random slopes, we fitted two alternative linear mixed models in R (lme4 and lmerTest): (1) Satterthwaite degrees of freedom and -values, and (2) a model with a by-participant random slope for the acoustic descriptor: All scripts, pipelines, and raw model outputs are available in the companion analytical repository (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23216344). Odds ratios, 95% confidence intervals, and FDR-adjusted p-values for the significant ordinal associations are given in Supplemental Table S1; results for all 171 ordinal models are available in the companion repository. Unless otherwise specified, all p-values in this manuscript are Benjamini-Hochberg FDR-adjusted.

3. Results

>Results

3.1. Acoustic profile of the GEMScapes dataset

Feature extraction across the 38 tracks yielded 1,457 acoustic and spatial descriptors per track (temporal, rhythmic, spectral, cepstral, tonal, harmonic-percussive, and spatial domains). To avoid high-dimensional redundancy and to keep the psychoacoustic modeling interpretable, we evaluated a curated, low-redundancy subset of 19 descriptors.

The Pearson correlation matrix of these 19 descriptors (Fig. 1) showed broad independence across domains, with a few natural acoustic couplings: spectral centroid mean and SD (r = 0.782), Onset Strength SD and rhythmic entropy (r = -0.632), integrated loudness and percussive energy SD (r = 0.605), spectral centroid SD and MFCC 1 SD (r = 0.584), and stereo width and phase correlation SD (r = 0.565). Across domains, all pairwise correlations were moderate (|r| < 0.65), and the feature space was acceptably conditioned (κ = 90.8; condition index = 9.5), with collinearity concentrated in the spectral centroid mean/SD pair (maximum VIF = 14.7).

Agglomerative hierarchical clustering with Ward's minimum-variance criterion on the 19 standardized descriptors partitioned the 38 tracks into three acoustic clusters (Fig. 2).

Cluster separation was weak (mean silhouette = 0.07 for k = 3; the highest value, 0.16, was obtained for k = 2), so the partition is used as a descriptive grouping of the tracks rather than as evidence of discrete acoustic types. Cluster 1 (N = 7) grouped tracks with prominent attack transients (high Onset Strength SD and percussive energy SD) and brighter spectra (high spectral centroid mean and SD), together with lower harmonic dominance and narrower stereo width. Cluster 2 (N = 17) comprised tracks dominated by sustained harmonic and tonal structure, with high harmonic dominance, pronounced spectral contrast, high key strength, and low chroma entropy. Cluster 3 (N = 14) captured expansive ambient soundscapes defined by wide stereo width, high rhythmic entropy, and pronounced spatial modulation (high ILD SD and phase correlation SD), with attenuated attack transients and minimal percussive energy.

Descriptive statistics confirm the largely non-pulsed, textural acoustic profile of GEMScapes. Temporally, the tracks had diffuse rhythmic structure. Onset strength, which has no absolute scale, averaged 0.85 (SD = 0.19), with a mean within-track SD of 0.84 (SD = 0.62); rhythmic entropy, normalized to [0, 1] with 1 indicating that no tempo dominates, averaged 0.84 (SD = 0.12), which reflects evolving soundscapes rather than periodic metrical grids. Dynamically, the tracks had a controlled energy profile, with a mean dynamic range of 13.72 dB (SD = 5.23 dB; difference between the 95th and 5th percentiles of RMS energy) and a mean integrated loudness of -16.40 LUFS (SD = 2.99 LUFS). Spectrally, energy was concentrated in the low-to-mid registers (mean spectral centroid = 1,465 Hz, SD = 806 Hz). Spatially, the tracks exhibited expansive soundstages

3.2. Human affective evaluation of the GEMScapes dataset

We collected 816 trial evaluations from 65 participants in 68 listening sessions across 36 tracks using the GEMS-9 (Jacobsen et al., 2025). Stimulus affective profiles were summarized with medians (Fig. 3) and interquartile ranges (IQR). Individual tracks The original GEMS framework groups music-induced emotions into three second-order factors: Sublimity (Wonder, Transcendence, Tenderness, Nostalgia, Peacefulness), Vitality (Joyful Activation, Power), and Unease (Tension, Sadness) (Zentner et al., 2008).

To examine co-occurrence across GEMScapes, we computed Spearman rank correlations on per-track median ratings (N = 36; Fig. the lowest maximum aggregated medians (2.5 and 3.0, respectively; Fig. 3), which suggests that they acted as secondary affective nuances rather than dominant emotions in this dataset.

Exploratory demographic comparisons in the subsample with demographic data (N = 55 participants) were performed at the participant level (median of each participant's 12 or 24 ratings per dimension; two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction across the nine dimensions). No GEMS dimension differed by formal musical training (all FDR-adjusted p = 1.000) or by sex (all FDR-adjusted p ≥ 0.212).

Given the small subgroups (e.g., 17 participants with significant musical training), these null results should be interpreted with caution, and they do not imply the absence of listener-specific variability, which the variance partitioning below quantifies.

3.3. Crossed linear mixed-effects models and variance decomposition

We first cross-referenced the unsupervised acoustic clusters (Fig. 2) with the dominant emotion of each track (the dimension with the highest median rating, ties broken by the mean rating; Supplemental Fig. S1), which showed alignment with arousal and soundstage spatialization. Cluster 1 (N = 7), defined by prominent attack transients and brighter spectra, contained mostly high-arousal, activating pieces: 5 of its 7 tracks had Joyful Activation (3 tracks) or Power (2 tracks) as the dominant emotion. Contemplative, low-arousal states concentrated in the harmonically dominated tonal branch (Cluster 2, N = 17), where 11 of 17 tracks had a Sublimity dimension as the dominant emotion:

Transcendence (4 tracks), Nostalgia (4), Peacefulness (2), and Tenderness (1). Cluster 3 (N = 14), the expansive ambient branch, spanned immersive soundscapes that alternated between serene contemplation (Peacefulness and Transcendence; 6 tracks) and dark atmospheric suspense (Tension; 3 tracks). Because 16 of the 36 rated tracks tie on their highest median, these counts depend on the tie-breaking rule and should be read as indicative. This loose correspondence between acoustic clusters and dominant emotions motivates trial-level mixed models to identify the continuous acoustic correlates of each emotion.

To identify these correlates, we evaluated the 19 curated descriptors against all nine GEMS dimensions (19 ×9 = 171 crossed LMMs). After Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction, nine models showed significant fixed effects (adjusted p < 0.05; Table 1, Fig. 5) across six emotional dimensions. These predictors converge on three physical themes: To quantify the influence of the stimulus versus idiosyncratic listener calibration, we partitioned variance across all dimensions (Table 2). Stimulus-driven variance exceeded listener variance in six of the nine dimensions and peaked for Tension (46.1% stimulus vs. 8.8% listener variance). Transcendence (18.6% vs. 22.7%) marked the inflection point at which listener variance began to exceed stimulus variance. At the other extreme, individual listener differences dominated Sadness (29.2% listener vs. 11.2% stimulus) and Wonder (31.7% vs.

8.0%), accounting for roughly 2.6 and 4 times more variance, respectively, than the music itself. Residual variance ranged from 45.1% to 60.3%, reflecting single-trial measurement error and unmodeled participant × track interactions.

3.4. Robustness validation: consensus profiling, ordinal modeling, and alternative LMM specifications

The three sensitivity analyses described in Section 2.5 gave results that converge with the primary LMMs.

Track-level consensus. Mean ratings per track were correlated with all 19 descriptors across the 171 pairs (Supplemental Figs. S2 and S3) with FDR correction. The analysis yielded nine significant associations (|r| = 0.50-0.65), which replicated all nine associations from the trial-level LMMs with identical signs and comparable relative magnitudes. With survey version partialled out (df = 32), the same nine associations remained significant after FDR adjustment. Unadjusted and partial correlation coefficients were virtually identical across the 171 pairs (r = 0.995; median absolute difference = 0.01), so macro-level stimulus norms converge with the trial-level mixedeffects results and the survey blocking design does not confound them.

Ordinal modeling. Predictor signs and relative magnitudes in the CLMMs agreed closely with the linear LMM estimates: directional sign agreement was 98.8% (169 of 171 models), and the correlation between linear slopes (β₁) and ordinal log-odds (log OR) was r = 0.98. All nine associations significant in the primary LMMs remained significant in the CLMMs under both conservative stimulus-level inference (Student's t, df = 32; 11 significant pairs in total; Supplemental Table S1) and asymptotic Wald z inference (17 pairs in total). Under the df = 32 criterion, only two additional associations reached significance: Peacefulness was negatively predicted by Spectral Centroid Mean (OR = 0.48), and Sadness was positively predicted by HPSS Harmonic Dominance Mean (OR = 1.73). Three models showed numerical non-convergence, none involving a significant predictor. This close correspondence indicates that the main psychoacoustic findings are robust to response-scale discretization and floor effects.

Alternative LMM specifications. Satterthwaite degrees of freedom (range 29.1-34.9, median 32.2) yielded the same nine significant associations after FDR correction. Adding by-participant random slopes for each descriptor left all nine associations significant, with negligible changes in standard errors (median standard-error ratio = 1.01, maximum = 1.11). With only 12 tracks per session, the data contain little information on how each participant's sensitivity to a descriptor differs from the average, and in 81 of the 171 models this random-slope variance could not be estimated reliably (singular fit). This supports the simpler crossed random-intercept specification used in the primary analysis.

Full model outputs and diagnostics for all 171 specifications are in the companion analytical repository.

4. Discussion

In this study, we related the acoustic features of 36 original ambient and cinematic tracks to the aesthetic emotions reported by listeners. As these pieces lack lyrics and have little metric regularity, their emotional character is likely to be carried by timbre, dynamics, texture, and spatial image rather than by words or rhythm. Six of the nine GEMS-9 dimensions showed consistent associations with specific acoustic descriptors. Because the descriptors vary together across tracks rather than independently, and all tracks were written by a single composer, these results describe associations rather than causal effects.

The emotions also differed in how much listeners agreed on them (Table 2). Agreement was highest for emotions at both ends of the arousal dimension, such as Tension and Joyful Activation on one side and Peacefulness and Tenderness on the other; for Tension, the track accounted for 46.1% of rating variance and the listener for only 8.8%. At the other extreme, Sadness and Wonder varied mainly between listeners (for Wonder, 8.0% vs. 31.7%), which may reflect personal associations, mood, or individual use of the rating scale. These emotions are therefore harder to target through the acoustic properties of a stimulus alone.

The co-occurrence of emotions across tracks (Fig. 4) only partly matched the original GEMS structure (Zentner et al., 2008). The clearest departure was Sadness, which grouped with the contemplative emotions rather than with Tension; this fits the idea that sadness in music is often experienced as a calm, pleasurable melancholy rather than as real distress (Taruffi & Koelsch, 2014). Wonder showed the opposite shift, correlating with Tension rather than with the calm emotions of the Sublimity factor.

4.1. Spectral variability and Tension

Tension was associated with how much the spectrum changed over time rather than with its average character. Its only significant predictor was the variability of spectral tilt (MFCC 1 SD; Table 1, Fig. 6), which reflects changes in the balance between low-and high-frequency energy and is related to fluctuations in brightness (r = 0.58 with Spectral Centroid SD; Fig. 1). Brightness itself, indexed by the mean spectral centroid (Schubert, 2004), did not predict Tension: tracks #012 and #028, for example, were relatively bright (spectral centroid mean in the upper third of the dataset) but spectrally stable (MFCC 1 SD in the lowest fifth), and received minimal Tension ratings (Mdn = 1.0).

This pattern is compatible with accounts in which changing sounds capture attention and raise arousal. Brainstem reflexes respond to sudden or changing acoustic events that may signal something important (Juslin, 2013), and unpredictable changes can violate auditory expectations (Huron, 2006), whereas a stable spectrum may allow listeners to habituate.

Continuous variation in psychoacoustic features has also been linked to moment-tomoment changes in felt emotion (Coutinho & Cangelosi, 2011). Because we collected no physiological data, these mechanisms remain hypotheses.

4.2. Percussive variability and Joyful Activation

Joyful Activation was associated with a different kind of variability. Its only significant predictor was the variability of percussive energy (HPSS percussive energy SD; Table 1, Fig. 6): tracks in which transient energy fluctuated more received higher Joyful Activation ratings. This agrees with structural accounts in which acoustic energy and transient events are primary cues for activation in music (Gabrielsson & Lindström, 2010). In beat-based music, such effects are often attributed to motor entrainment and its links with reward (Salimpoor et al., 2011; Vuilleumier & Trost, 2015). Our predictor, however, measures how much percussive energy varies, not whether it follows a regular pulse, so whether entrainment contributes to this association remains to be tested.

4.3. Acoustic stability and introspective states

The more introspective emotions showed the opposite profile: less variability and, for Transcendence, a wider stereo image (Table 1, Fig. 6). Transcendence was the only dimension associated with a spatial descriptor. It increased with stereo width (Stereo Width Mean) and decreased with the variability of onset strength (Onset Strength SD), so it was rated higher for wide, enveloping textures without marked attacks. Peacefulness and Nostalgia were associated with spectral stability: both decreased with fluctuations in brightness (Spectral Centroid SD), and Nostalgia also decreased with spectral-tilt variability (MFCC 1 SD).

One possible interpretation draws on predictive accounts of music perception, in which marked, regular events continuously engage prediction and motor preparation (Koelsch et al., 2019). Smooth, stable textures offer few such anchors and may leave attention free to turn inward. This would be consistent with evidence that low-arousal musical emotions such as Peacefulness, Nostalgia, and Sadness engage ventromedial prefrontal regions that overlap with the default network (Trost et al., 2012), and that music can promote mindwandering and change DMN centrality (Taruffi et al., 2017).

Wonder and Sadness, the two emotions that depended most on the listener, differed in their acoustic profiles. Wonder had no significant predictor, consistent with its small stimulus share (8.0%; Table 2). Sadness, in contrast, was associated with darker and more stable timbre (lower Spectral Centroid Mean and SD, two strongly correlated descriptors), although these were the smallest of the nine effects (|β₁| ≈ 0.2). The ordinal models also linked Sadness to higher harmonic dominance (Section 3.4), but this association was not significant in the primary linear models.

4.4. Power: tentative tonal and harmonic trends

Although Power showed substantial stimulus variance (24.5%; Table 2), no descriptor predicted it after FDR correction. The strongest non-significant candidates were a larger Tonnetz fifths radius, lower harmonic dominance, and lower upper-mid spectral contrast (Fig. 5). Lower harmonic dominance reached significance only in the ordinal models with asymptotic Wald inference, not with the conservative stimulus-level test (full results in the companion repository).

These trends point in a direction suggested by research on film music. Traditional accounts link tonal expectation and harmonic resolution to positive valence and reduced anxiety (Huron, 2006; Margulis, 2005), whereas in modern cinematic scoring, impressions of vastness and power are often created by acoustic roughness, broadband textures, or ambiguous modal shifts that lower harmonic dominance (Lahdelma & Eerola, 2020; Lehman, 2018). Because none of these associations reached significance in the primary models, this interpretation remains speculative and requires replication.

4.5. Implications for sound design and neurocognitive research

GEMScapes provides acoustically characterized stimuli with normative emotional ratings, together with an estimate of how much each emotion depends on the stimulus rather than on the listener. For sound design, the associations reported here could serve as initial guidelines for adaptive audio and interactive soundscapes, particularly for emotions on which listeners agreed most, such as Tension and Peacefulness. The association of a wide stereo image and smooth onsets with Transcendence, for example, suggests a starting point for spatial audio in immersive VR, pending replication with music by other composers and with other listener groups.

For experimental and clinical research, the acoustic profiles associated with Peacefulness and Transcendence (low attack variability, a stable spectral centroid, and a wide stereo image) offer reference points for selecting or designing stimuli, including for closed-loop, biofeedback-driven VR environments (Agres et al., 2021; Benítez et al., 2026). Because the stimuli are described parametrically, future fMRI and EEG studies could vary these properties systematically and test whether they modulate DMN activity and connectivity, which can change with music listening (Wilkins et al., 2014).

4.6. Limitations

Although the main results were robust to data aggregation, ordinal modeling, and alternative model specifications (Section 3.4), several limitations define their scope.

First, all 38 tracks were composed and produced by a single author. This was an intentional choice to ensure consistent production and to avoid prior familiarity, but it also limits stylistic variety to one composer's musical vocabulary, so some associations may reflect specific sound-design habits rather than features of the genre as a whole. The crossed random intercepts account for track-specific idiosyncrasies, but they cannot separate composer style from genre; replicating these analyses with ambient music by other composers is an important next step.

Second, ratings were collected online, at participants' homes and without supervision.

Although participants were instructed to use headphones, we could not control the listening environment, the headphones used (whose frequency response differs between models), or the playback level, which adds unmodeled auditory variance. In addition, presentation order was fixed within each survey version, so order effects are confounded with track identity. Listeners nevertheless showed no clear signs of fatigue: excerpts late in the sequence still received some of the highest ratings for contrasting emotions (e.g., Joyful Activation for track #032 at position 9, and Nostalgia for #009 and Tension for #027 at position 11; all Mdn = 4.0). Laboratory replications with calibrated playback would help assess finer timbral effects.

Third, the sample was mainly composed of young adults (M age = 24.7 years, SD = 9.03, among the 55 participants with demographic data) without significant formal musical training (69.1%). The results therefore describe non-expert listeners, and future studies should include older, musically trained, and cross-cultural groups.

Finally, because acoustic features vary only between tracks, the effective sample size for testing them is the 36 rated tracks rather than the 816 ratings. Weaker associations may therefore have gone undetected; Tenderness, for example, showed substantial stimulus variance (Table 2) but no significant predictor. Detecting such effects would require larger sets of stimuli. The exploratory demographic comparisons were similarly limited by the small size of the subgroups.

5. Conclusions

GEMScapes provides 38 original ambient and cinematic tracks with acoustic descriptors and normative GEMS-9 ratings, openly available for research on music and emotion. In these tracks, emotions were associated mainly with how the sound changes over time and how widely it spreads across the stereo field, and some emotions depended far more on the listener than on the music. Both points are worth considering when selecting or designing auditory stimuli for affective and neurocognitive research.

Data and Code Availability Statement

The GEMScapes dataset is openly available on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21263434). It contains the 38 tracks as uncompressed stereo WAV files (48 kHz, 16-bit); the acoustic feature matrices computed from the stereo signal (features_stereo.csv, 1,457 descriptors) and from the mono downmix (features_mono.csv, 1,371 descriptors); the Python feature-extraction pipeline; the anonymized GEMS-9 ratings; and an HTML report for each track with Mel spectrograms, acoustic timelines, and, for the 36 rated tracks, the distribution of emotion ratings.

The Python and R code for all statistical analyses is archived in a companion Zenodo repository (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23216344). It is organized in three modules: survey statistics (01_Survey_Statistics), crossed LMMs and variance partitioning (02_Linear_Mixed_Effects_Models), and the robustness and sensitivity analyses described in Sections 2.3 and 2.5 (03_Robustness_Validation). The repository includes the input data, scripts, dependencies, and pre-computed outputs needed to reproduce these analyses; the exploratory demographic comparisons (Section 3.2) are not included.
